# OpenVMM runtime: fifth release candidate

This release enables a bounded set of KVM paravirtual features for ordinary
Linux VMs and requires KVM to enforce their CPUID policy on every vCPU. Linux
guests can use KVM clocks, steal time, PV interrupt handling, spinlocks, TLB
flush, IPIs, polling control and scheduler yield when the host supports them.

## Host compatibility

**Linux hosts must support `KVM_CAP_ENFORCE_PV_FEATURE_CPUID`.** If the capability
is unavailable or cannot be enabled, VM startup fails instead of silently
running without enforcement. This also applies to the KVM kernel inside a
provider VM when using nested virtualization.

CPUID advertisement alone does not block a malicious guest from accessing KVM
PV interfaces. This release enables the kernel's enforcement for feature-gated
PV operations. It is not a general MSR/hypercall firewall or a claim that all
hypervisor attack paths have been audited.

## Changes

- Expose only explicitly selected, host-supported KVM PV feature bits. Do not
  advertise async page faults, migration controls, extended MSI destinations,
  unknown future features, or the realtime scheduling hint.
- Apply the policy through the existing commit-pinned OpenVMM 0.4.0 checkout,
  patching both `virt_kvm` and its `kvm` ioctl wrapper. Keep one OpenVMM dependency
  source and the workspace lockfile.
- Add Linux KVM regressions that run two VMs concurrently, each with four vCPUs.
  The guest executes real MSR reads/writes to verify rejection of excluded
  async-PF operations, invalid PV EOI addresses and reserved poll-control bits.
  Allowed PV operations and subsequent file, network, process and shutdown
  checks must still succeed.
- Build the test-only MSR module from the same checksum-pinned package as the
  guest kernel. It is loaded only inside test guests and is excluded from the
  production initramfs and release packages.

## Validation

Local direct-host and nested-KVM tests passed, including the concurrent guest
probes. As a negative control, the previous unenforced PV build accepted an
excluded async-PF MSR read, and the new regression correctly detected it.
This demonstrates enforcement of the tested restrictions, not a prior data leak
or VM escape. These are bounded tests, not a prolonged denial-of-service or
resource-leak assessment.

Publication requires Linux and Windows native checks, the RustSec audit,
Linux KVM integration tests, packaging and checksum verification. Actual Windows
WHP guest execution remains unverified.
